Threat.value: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.
The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

issues.item: Threat: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
issues.explanation: For a captivity trauma profile, the threat pattern is dominated by loud sounds/startle and false alarms, but 'checking if someone is following me' implies a stalking/pursuit-based danger context that is not supported by the listed triggers or memory items. With strong Threat → Triggers and Memory → Triggers links, the threat content should connect plausibly to the trigger set; here the pursuit-focused checking stands out as clinically mismatched.

issues.item: Memory: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
issues.explanation: Within the memory node, recurrent replay and uncontrolled intrusions fit the formulation and trauma type, but intense shame on recall introduces a self-evaluative appraisal theme that is otherwise absent. Given that Negative Appraisals is not represented and Threat → Negative Appraisals / Memory → Negative Appraisals are inactive, this item does not cohere well with the otherwise sensory-intrusive memory profile.

For captivity trauma, 'similar cars' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile unless transport vehicles were a clearly central part of the trauma. The other selected trigger items and all Threat/Memory items point to a general captivity-style pattern of somatic/tactile cueing, intrusive replay, terror on recall, and hypervigilance to sudden sounds. A car-specific visual trigger stands out as insufficiently connected to the rest of this formulation and is the one item a clinician would most likely question.

vignette:
Liam, a 45-year-old journalist, described the last six months as living in the "epilogue of a story I can't stop re-reading." The assignment had been his most ambitious: a deep dive into an insurgent group in a volatile, remote region. It ended with three weeks in a dark, damp cellar. He was home now, physically safe, but the cellar had come with him. The trauma began with the smell of cheap, sour alcohol on the breath of the man who'd thrown the hood over his head, and it was that scent that now seemed to follow him everywhere. His captors were often drunk, their movements unpredictable, their grips bruising and rough. For days on end, he was forced to kneel with his head bowed, a position that left a searing, chronic pain in his neck that has never fully subsided.

In the first few weeks after his release, Liam tried to force a return to normalcy. He went back to the bustling newsroom, telling his editor and concerned colleagues he was fine. But he was not. He had become a man perpetually braced for impact. Every unexpected sound-a door slamming down the hall, a car backfiring on the street below his office window-sent a jolt of raw adrenaline through him. He found himself constantly scanning faces in a crowd, mapping exits, judging every person who walked too close. He knew, rationally, that he was in Manhattan, not a war zone, but his body refused to believe it. This state of constant, exhausting hypervigilance felt like a necessary shield, but it was also a magnet for the past. The more he remained on high alert, the more the memories of the cellar found their way through the cracks in his concentration. The feeling of being in imminent danger seemed to call them forth, and they would arrive without warning, hijacking his senses.

The memories are not fleeting images but full sensory replays. He described them as a film that plays over and over, one he cannot turn off. The darkness of the room, the rough texture of the burlap hood, the muffled, angry voices-it all forces its way into his mind, bringing with it the same gut-twisting terror he felt then. A deadline at work would be looming, and suddenly he would be back in the cellar, convinced he was about to be executed. These intrusive replays have made his world a minefield. After one of these episodes, his sensitivity to his triggers becomes painfully acute. The dull ache in his neck, a constant companion, flares into a sharp, debilitating pain, as if he were still being held down. He feels the ghost of his captors' hands on him, and the most innocent physical contact becomes unbearable. The memory primes his body for a threat that is no longer there.

This vicious cycle now governs his life. His constant feeling of being on guard, of being unsafe, not only triggers the memories but also makes him exquisitely sensitive to the world around him. His wife, Anna, once tried to welcome him home with a hug from behind; he instinctively threw an elbow back, nearly striking her before he registered who it was. The look on her face, a mixture of shock and hurt, still haunts him. He saw he was becoming as unpredictable and frightening as his captors had been. Now, he flinches from her touch, creating a painful distance between them. The smell of alcohol on someone's breath at a restaurant is enough to make him bolt for the door, his heart hammering against his ribs. He has started taking only desk assignments at the paper, unable to face the unpredictable nature of field reporting that was once the lifeblood of his career.

Liam came to therapy after Anna told him, her voice quiet with exhaustion, that she felt she was living with a ghost. He fears she is right. He is trapped in that cellar, and he is terrified he will lose his wife and the career he loves because he cannot find his way out. He doesn't want to be a ghost; he wants to be the man he was before, a man who could hold his wife's hand and walk into a crowded room without feeling like the walls were about to cave in. He is desperate, he said, to finally end the story.
